Ventral coloration is similar in both species in escarpment populations and could not be used as a distinguishing characteristic. Both are dark-bellied and have somewhat lighter threats.
After jordani and glutinosus were separated by pigmentation, individuals were measured, dissected, and sexed. An attempt was made to determine whether the animals were sexually mature; this was generally more successful for males than for females. For the former, specimens were considered mature if the following criteria were satisfied: (1) presence of a mental gland; (2) an abundance of orangecolored hedonic glands on the venter; (3) enlarged, pigmented testes with black, coiled sperm ducts. As large males possess these characteristics at all seasons of the year, there is probably little chance of confusing immature males with those that are mature but sexually inactive. For females, maturity is more difficult to ascertain, and the sole criterion was the condition of the ovaries. In small and presumably immature individuals, the ovaries are invariably small and compact, with tiny. pale white oucytes. Out of the egg-laying season, the ovaries of the larger females are relatively larger, and at least some of the oneytes are slightly enlarged and yolky. In
many specimens the ovaries are long and contain few orbites; these probably represent females that have recently outposites. Few females of either species had enlarged eggs ready for deposition. No differences were noted between the gonads of the two species.
Size and sex data are presented in Table II. As shown, glutinosus attains a larger size than fordani, the largest glutinosus being over 10 mm, longer than the largest jurdani. Sexual maturit, also occurs at a larger size in glutinosus. In both species the females mature at a larger size than the males; consequently the average size of mature females is greater than the average for mature males. In jurdani there appears to be geographic variation in size, even within the limited area of the escarpment.
Variation in Pigmentation in Plethodon jordani
In his study of P. jordani elemsome, Schwartz (1957) limited the range of this subspecies to the locassee Valley of Oconee County, South Carolina. Gordon (1960) noted the occurrence of brassy pigment in melovouris populations of jordani in the vicinity of Highlands, North Carolina. In the present study I found that dursal brassy flecking and lateral white spotting occur in many escarpment populations, and that the trend of variation is such that drawing geographic homolaries to the subspecies elemsome and melocyntris is impossible.
